title: Beatrix and the Language
premise: Hazel Amberdale has spent eleven years writing postcards to Beatrix Vane at an address that burned down in 2009 — letters he never sent to a woman who may never have existed outside his guilt. When the Vane house goes up for auction, Hazel discovers the estate includes a sealed deposition Beatrix left naming him as the sole witness to her brother's death, and the auction cannot close until the document is 'translated' from the private shorthand the siblings invented as children. As developers, lawyers, and Beatrix's estranged daughter close in on the property, Hazel must decode the sentence that will either convict or absolve him. He finishes the translation on the eve of the sale, reads it aloud at the closing table, and chooses to let the house go — signing away his claim so the land becomes a public garden, carrying the sentence home at last as something lived with rather than hidden.
about_author: Dominic Underhill is a former court stenographer from the Yorkshire coast whose debut novel drew on fifteen years of transcribing other people's confessions. He writes in a converted signal box and claims he can no longer remember which of his memories are his own.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. We meet him in his rented room, writing his 4,000th postcard to Beatrix at the burned address, then learn the Vane house is listed for auction by a development firm. A lawyer's letter arrives demanding he appear as 'interested party.' The emotional beat is dread disguised as routine — Hazel realizes the past has found a forwarding address.

chapters.title: The Shorthand of Siblings
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, with flashbacks to childhood summers at the Vane house where he, Beatrix, and her brother Tomas built a private language. At the pre-auction inspection he finds the sealed deposition and recognizes the script. Beatrix's daughter, Imogen, confronts him, suspecting he's after the property. The beat is vertigo: memory and evidence beginning to disagree.

chapters.title: What the Sentence Says
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV under mounting pressure as the auction date nears and Imogen, now uneasy ally, helps him reconstruct the code. Decoding reveals Tomas's death was not the accident Hazel testified it was — and that Beatrix knew, and forgave him in the same breath she condemned him. The climax arrives at the closing: Hazel reads the translated sentence aloud, refusing both the lawyers' silence and his own.

chapters.title: Tenant No Longer
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, weeks later. The sale closes without him; the garden clause holds because Imogen honors what he read aloud. He writes one final postcard — addressed to himself this time — and moves out of his rented room into a flat he actually owns. The resolution is quiet justice: not acquittal but authorship, a man finally living inside his own sentence.
